It seemed to me it lay in this: that everything should be put away in a cupboard; that no object, no moulding on the wall or on the doors or furniture should remain outside to catch one speck of the dirt and grime of our cities; that all the dirt should reach the floor whence the electric suction sweeper should remove it.

brief_context: Mentioned as the author of 'My Philosophy of Industry'.
brief_extract: If that home really represented what woman to-day wants, it can only be because she has not thought of the possible. Henry Ford, in his recently published “My Philosophy of Industry,” deals briefly with this theme. His solution appears to be to follow in the case of daily meals what has already been done in that of bread, that is, have them prepared and cooked outside and delivered hot at the appropriate moment; the service articles, plates, cups, cutlery, are presumably to be collected and cleaned at the central factory.

House, Newcastle-on-Tyne, where a film and demonstration gave the girls some idea

title: Miss
brief_context: Conducted a demonstration of electric household appliances for visitors.
article_title: A Day in an All-Electric House.
brief_extract:
Thus ended “a perfect day in an all-electric house.”
This, then, is what we saw on the film, but it is better to describe it first so that we do know something about electricity before we use it for so many things. We were welcomed in the demonstration theatre by Miss Holm and in a few moments the demonstration had started. Miss Holm said she would do some washing for us, also some ironing, and she would bake an apple tart and make some bread, and also cook some vegetables.

title: Miss
brief_context: Demonstrated electric sweepers and floor appliances for the visitors.
brief_extract: We paid a short visit to the rooms where there were electric sweepers with their various additions and electric floor polishers and floor washers. The party had now divided into two sections, one following the showroom gentleman and one accompanied by Miss Holm, who demonstrated for us on the above-mentioned appliances. Time was short, so we returned downstairs, saw the accountancy department, also the repair department and the electric telephone, where calls could be put through to any part of Carliol House.

brief_context: Designed the beautiful fountain for Carliol House.
brief_extract: We saw ovens and the electric washers and mangles such as were used during the demonstrations and exactly like the one seen on the film. Finally the two parties assembled at the beautiful fountain designed for Carliol House by a girl student of Armstrong College.

brief_context: Hostess demonstrating her modern all-electric kitchen and home.
brief_extract:
58
The Electrical Age

How I loved that little kitchen, with its built-in, glass-fronted dresser, its large well-ventilated corner cupboard, its basin and sink, each provided with constant hot water, and its white " tiled " walls reflecting the light from a 40-watt inside-frosted lamp, so placed that it illuminated the interior of the cupboard when open. " I thought at first that I could manage with a lower wattage in a room only 6 feet square," Mary informed me, " but I found a dim light had a most depressing effect when I arrived home tired after my day's work, and the extra fillip to my spirits is well worth the very small extra cost of current. Here again," she confessed, " I should like another small outlet for my iron, but have to manage with this adaptor fixed to the lighting unit above the shade, with a switch on it which enables the iron to be used either with the light on or off.

article_title: Electricity without Tears - A Suggested approach to the Electricity of the Home.
brief_extract: PART I. Once upon a time there was a boy whose name was Bob. Bob was a nice little fellow, but he had one sad failing which sometimes led him into trouble—he was rather too fond of eating sweet things.

brief_context: A little old man who takes Bob to a strange country.
article_title: Electricity without Tears - A Suggested approach to the Electricity of the Home.
brief_extract: He kept on saying to himself, "I feel so fat, I feel so fat. I wish I could get thin again." Bob must have fallen asleep at last, and begun to dream, because there suddenly appeared at the side of his bed a little old man with a long beard, who said, "Bob, if you really mean what you say, I will take you to my country, where they make fat people thin." "Oh, please do," cried Bob, "I would go anywhere to get thin once more." "Very well," said Slim, for that was the little old man's name, "get out of bed and come with me." So Bob rolled off his bed on to the floor and, before he realised what was happening, he began to sink through the floor, down and down and down. At last he found himself standing with Slim in a strange country which seemed to be inhabited by funny little men who were all rushing about at a tremendous rate as if they were in a desperate hurry to get somewhere before it was too late.

brief_extract: Let us now get back to the other things mentioned in our story. Look at a common electric pocket torch and you will see that it has all the features which Bob saw from the top of the tree. Where is the Feeding House?

brief_context: A character mentioned in the story used for metaphors.
article_title: Electricity without Tears: A Suggested approach to the Electricity of the Home.
brief_extract: Where is the Feeding House? You will guess that this is the battery, where the procession of electricity derives its energy and driving force, which Slim spoke of as magic pudding. You will see at the top of the battery two metal strips; what would Bob call them?

brief_context: Fictional character used in an analogy to explain electrical concepts.
brief_extract: Now we come to the method used for stopping the flow of electricity. In the story, Slim blocked up the path at one point when he wanted to stop the procession of running men. We can produce the same result in the electrical path by making a gap in the metal, because the electricity can only run through the metal wire, and cannot pass through the air forming a gap in the wire.

Reference to analogies for direct and alternating current types.
article_title: Electric Clocks which Regulate and Wind Themselves.
brief_extract: The new All Mains clock, known as the "Synclock," works on an entirely new principle which is quite novel, but by readers of "Electrical Age" it will be easily grasped. They already know all about the difference between direct current and alternating current; how with direct current Bob's "fat men" and "thin men" (see the "Electrical Age" for January and April) run continuously round in the same direction, whereas with alternating current they run first in one direction and then in the other. And in spite of their corpulence they do this at such a prodigious speed that they get right round the circle and back again fifty times in every second.

brief_context: Famous clockmaker who created the original 1699 clock movement.
brief_extract: It may be added that it is quite easy to convert any existing clock into a "Synclock" or, alternatively, to fit a "Synclock" movement into an antique clock-case, the "works" of which may long since have had to be discarded. A recent case may be cited of a fine old Tompion clock of 1699, which, after a useful life of 230 years, steadfastly refused to go. The clock experts drew long faces and prescribed new sets of wheels throughout.

title: King
role: King of England; King of Scotland; King of Ireland
brief_context: Reign in which the Tompion clock was originally built.
brief_extract:
But there seemed no alternative, until the "Synclock" motor solved the difficulty. Without destroying a single wheel, the little motor was connected to one of them, and the clock once again started upon its useful career, keeping time with an accuracy of a few seconds a week, an accuracy never even dreamt of by Tompion of old

It is interesting to speculate upon what the future may have in store for this old clock, built in the reign of William and Mary (only forty years, in fact, after the Fire of London) and electrified in the reign of King George V. Perhaps in another 250 years, clocks and watches will be driven and controlled by radiant energy from the sun itself.

title: Sir
brief_context: Recalled in relation to constructing the Forth Bridge.
article_title: The New President, LADY MOIR, O.B.E.
brief_extract: In my memory it was considered a novelty to see a great engineering work lighted by electricity—a notable example being the Forth Bridge, lit by electric arc lamps to make it possible to carry on the work of construction night and day ; and this was done summer and winter. Even then breakdowns were somewhat frequent, and I can recall Sir William Arrol when the arc lights failed admonishing his electric engineer and accusing him with kindly sarcasm of " looking for them with a candle." At that time no electric motor could be relied on for driving machinery with certainty. Electrical cranes were unheard of, and electrical pumps and machinery, so easily obtained to-day, were unprocurable.

title: Sir; Bart.
brief_context: Husband of Lady Moir and a foremost civil engineer.
article_title: The New President, LADY MOIR, O.B.E.
brief_extract: Lady Moir, O.B.E., was elected President of the Electrical Association for Women at the Annual General Meeting held at the Park Lane Hotel on April 17th. Lady Moir, who is a Past President of the Women's Engineering Society and a Founder Member of the Electrical Association for Women, has often described herself as an " Engineers by Marriage." As wife of one of the foremost Civil Engineers of the day, Sir Ernest Moir, Bart., she has travelled all over the world with her husband in his work in connection with the building of Bridges, Tunnels, Docks and Harbours. Lady Moir's interest in Engineering was aroused during the War, when she was one of the organisers of the Week-End Relief Work, herself working the weekend shift, and being a successful lathe operator for over eighteen months.

title: Miss
associated_organisation: Electrical Association for Women; Board of Education
brief_context: Director of the Association who organised the first electrical school.
brief_extract: It is a great satisfaction that the Board of Education at Whitehall has appreciated the need of instructing the teachers in the Domestic Science Centres in a knowledge of electricity and its applications to the home. Last year the first school on the Domestic Uses of Electricity held under the auspices of the Board of Education was organised and conducted by our Director, Miss Haslett, and proved to be a great success. The lecturers dealt with the many applications of electricity in the home in connection with cooking, heating, cleaning, and the students were also given some simple instruction on house wiring and household repairs.

title: Miss
associated_organisation: Glasgow Branch of the Electrical Association for Women
brief_context: Member of the Glasgow Branch who performed individual lecturing.
brief_extract: We should like to feel that the Scottish Board of Education, which has always been progressive, will realise that elementary electrical education is a subject which should be included in the curriculum of training for school teachers. A good deal of individual lecturing has been done by Miss Kennedy and members of our Glasgow Branch, but we feel the time has come when the matter should be taken up by the Scottish Educational Authorities. In addition to the work which we have done for the Board of Education, the Association has received requests from many Educational Authorities and Teachers' Associations throughout the country for advice and help on electrical training in the schools.

title: Miss
brief_context: Suggested as a contact for incorporating electrical training for servants.
brief_extract:
These posts are very well paid, but we have been unable to fill them as there appears to be no training of the necessary kind at the moment. We would like to suggest to Miss Bondfield, Minister of Labour, that in the Centres conducted by the Ministry of Labour for training domestic servants there should be included some knowledge on the use and maintenance of electrical appliances. With the introduction of electricity and science into the home we feel domestic service in the future should appeal to the educated girl, and we see through the agency of electricity the possibility of home management being regarded as a "skilled occupation."

I have indicated to you the three main directions in which as an Association we feel that electrical education is specially needed.

brief_context: Character in the metaphorical story of electricity.
article_title: Electricity without Tears: A Suggested approach to the Electricity of the Home.
brief_extract: The number of men who pass through the feeding-house in an hour is the same as the number of men who are passing along any part of the path in the same time—thus it will be exactly the same as the number of men who pass through the squeegee in an hour. If you think about it carefully, you will see that the number of men passing into the feeding-house (or going past any other place along the path where Bob was watching) per hour will give a sort of measure of the crowdedness of the procession. One man per hour would be a very "thin" procession indeed, while a million men per hour would be a dense hurrying crowd which we must picture as rushing along the path like a crowd in a street and not just one man behind another.

brief_context: The Watt unit is named after this engineering inventor.
brief_extract: Consequently, if we multiply the number of volts by the number of amperes, we shall get the total amount of pudding served each hour by the cook. We give a special name to this rate at which the pudding is supplied, and call it the Watt (the name of the great engineering inventor, James Watt). Thus the pudding supplied per hour is a certain number of watts, and we obtain this number by multiplying the number of volts by the number of amperes.

brief_extract: Among the many other trades which owe much to Faraday's discoveries are dyeing, electro-plating, work in which the liquefaction of gases plays its part and of course, electro-therapy. At the Annual Dinner of the Women's Engineering Society, held at the Lyceum Club, Lady Moir, O.B.E., in proposing the toast of "Michael Faraday," referred to the great influence his mother and his wife had on his life and his work. It was interesting to see that a woman's name appeared among those who were asked to speak in Faraday's honour, and it is significant of the times that women should take so prominent a part in honouring this great scientist ; perhaps one of the results of his work which would have pleased Faraday most is the simplification of household tasks which electricity has already achieved.

Realising that many individual members of the Association have contributed very considerably to its success by bringing in large numbers of new members, the President, Lady Moir, O.B.E., has decided to present a "Membership Cup" to the individual who who has brought in the largest number of new members in a year. brief_context: Former President of the Society, identified as the author.
Philosopher quoted regarding living according to reason and fashion.
brief_extract:
The chief one is fear—
a dread of the unusual, coupled with a
slavish adherence to the commonplace. Is
it not Seneca who says " that we live not
according to the light of reason, but after
the fashion of others ? " We so often hear
too much of the monotony of life, and too
little of the monotony of our surroundings,
and this monotony we bestow upon ourselves
through our adherence to drab colours,
inadequate lighting, and over-crowded
furnishing.

title: Lord
brief_context: Mentioned for his expression 'no damned merit' regarding courage of opinion.
brief_extract:
Simply made furniture
demands simply treated walls, and we can
learn much from the Japanese, who long
ago realised the merit of elegance, form, and
the value of space. Lord Melbourne used the expression " no
damned merit " in reference to something
deemed of great value by many others,
whereby he showed courage of opinion. Nowhere is such courage needed as by those
who are endeavouring to demonstrate that
there is still a great unexplored world before us
in the method and manner of the decoration
and arrangement in our present day houses
and those of the future.

brief_context: Mentioned as a comparison for polarizing modern strip lighting.
brief_extract: Artificial windows lighted from behind are highly useful and beautiful adjuncts to a room with dark corners, and those of you who know the glory of a stained glass window in the sunshine and how comparatively uninteresting it looks on a grey day will appreciate to the full the satisfaction to be derived from electrical sunshine falling always through it. In the dignified entrance hall concealed lighting is demonstrated to advantage ; various reception rooms and offices are fitted with the most modern strip lights which, like Epstein, one either loathes or adores ; and a completely furnished bathroom displays the latest in illuminated shaving mirrors calculated to send the most truculent of men to the breakfast table in pacific mood and with smooth face. But since lighting is but one of the lines—albeit perhaps the most fascinating of all—I must, with lamentable briefness, for space grows short, mention some of the other services which are placed at the disposal of the fortunate inhabitants of Brompton and Kensington.

title: Sultan

brief_extract: She has also travelled widely with him in India, America, and the West Indies, where they inspected the pitch lake which supplies bitumen for their cables. brief_context: Author of the 'poverty line' concept used in budgets.
brief_extract:
The Electrical Age 403

Rowntree's "poverty line," would require 41/3 a week, and anything less quite definitely means inadequate or sub-standard provision for basic human needs. This estimate includes an allowance of 9/- a week only for rent and nothing at all for such items as smoking, papers, stamps, or even train fares, and in London and other large cities the rent allowance would be found inadequate.

brief_context: His food value assessments are used as a basis.
brief_extract: ‘Man Values’ and Food Values. It is generally admitted that family budgets should be studied with a view to ascertaining the amount spent on food per man value of the family, taking Graham Lusk’s or the Medical Research Council’s assessments as a basis, but since it is plain that whatever the method adopted, the income is usually insufficient to provide proper nourishment, we have refrained from making the necessary somewhat intricate calculations. Professor Mottram, commenting on a group of budgets collected at random by the British Broadcasting Corporation in July, 1931, points out, however, that even where real food value efficiency is not possible, much could be achieved by a more scientific choice of diet.

title: Professor
associated_organisation: King's College London; British Broadcasting Corporation
brief_context: Commented on budgets collected by the BBC in 1931.
brief_extract: It is generally admitted that family budgets should be studied with a view to ascertaining the amount spent on food per man value of the family, taking Graham Lusk’s or the Medical Research Council’s assessments as a basis, but since it is plain that whatever the method adopted, the income is usually insufficient to provide proper nourishment, we have refrained from making the necessary somewhat intricate calculations. Professor Mottram, commenting on a group of budgets collected at random by the British Broadcasting Corporation in July, 1931, points out, however, that even where real food value efficiency is not possible, much could be achieved by a more scientific choice of diet. For instance, in one case he says “At the same expenditure nearly double the energy (as food), and double the body building material could have been bought if meat had been replaced by cheese.” The value of spreading information about food values and their cost would obviously be great, and this would appear rather to involve a better use being made of, and greater publicity being given to information already available than original research work.

brief_extract:
The Electrical Age 409

Independence for the Invalid
How Electricity Helps
By Stella Wolfe Murray,
who finds Electricity a life-saver, by making it her hand-maiden. Having found electricity a life-saver during two and a half years of invalidism, eighteen months of it actually in bed without the power to walk a few steps to the bathroom, and one year with that power regained, it occurred to me that other invalids might be interested to know the gadgets in use, and how they save the cost of a nurse and enable me to carry on with the minimum of domestic help.

brief_extract:
To a

BROADCASTING
HOUSE

A VISIT BY POST

by
Gladys F. Sharp

MY DEAR PHYLLIS,
It was most unfortunate that the B.B.C. issued such a limited number of invitations for the visit to Broadcasting House, and the only consolation I can offer you for being left out is the fact that you had as companions in distress some two hundred good and true members of the E.A.W.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding speculation on the brains of the public.
article_title: To a Disappointed Friend BROADCASTING HOUSE A VISIT BY POST
brief_extract: Better luck next time, perhaps, and in the meantime here is the description I promised you. When I first saw Broadcasting House my thought was: "If it hadn't been for the discovery of electricity this would never have been built." Of course, the mere passer-by might not think of that—probably would not—but I believe even the mere man-or-woman-in-the-street, whose brains are for ever a subject of speculation to the Sitwells of this world, would have become 'electrically-conscious'—lovely expression! —once the Commissionaire was safely passed and the innermost secrets of Broadcasting House his or hers for the looking.

brief_context: Author of Paradise Lost mentioned to describe depth.
article_title: To a Disappointed Friend BROADCASTING HOUSE A VISIT BY POST
brief_extract: We went straight down by lift to the very depths of the earth. It reminded me of Milton's "Paradise Lost" : "From morn till noon he fell, from noon till dewy eve." I don't remember just where Lucifer landed but our destination was the air conditioning plant—you know, the sort of thing kinemas brag about. The air is sucked in, filtered, washed, cooled or heated according to need and finally distributed throughout every nook and cranny of the building so that the veriest office boy may breathe through his mouth all day and find his lungs no wit the worse at the end.

title: Queen
brief_context: Mentioned regarding the period of legal reform for women.
brief_extract: In law in this country as recently as the end of the last century a woman's property passed in effect to her husband on marriage, and it was only in 1882 that a married woman obtained the right to carry on any business in her own name and to manage her own property. This was, of course, during the long reign of Queen Victoria and it was perhaps inevitable that during such a period with a lady at the head of the constitution reformation should take place in woman's position by law. During the same period, perhaps for the first time in this country, it became generally, if grudgingly conceded, that with the same opportunities as man woman might develop and generally be permitted to engage in some of the simpler of the intellectual pursuits.

brief_context: Mentioned as writing under a male pseudonym in 1850.
brief_extract: During the same period, perhaps for the first time in this country, it became generally, if grudgingly conceded, that with the same opportunities as man woman might develop and generally be permitted to engage in some of the simpler of the intellectual pursuits. It is significant to call to mind that as late as 1850 a woman novelist, George Eliot, was writing under a man's name because the public were not yet prepared to accept a book written by a woman as being worthy of consideration. I am going over these points because I wish you to realise to the full that even in this country, which we consider an enlightened one in such matters, it is only during very recent years that woman has come to be considered by man as the possessor of gifts which may equal or even excel his own.

brief_context: Discoverer of electromagnetic induction mentioned in the text.
brief_extract:
J. JENNINGS

The cartoons by "Mac" are reproduced by courtesy of the "Electrical Review."

It is just about one hundred years ago since Michael Faraday first made the discovery after years of thought and experiment and research that an electric current is set up or induced to flow in a wire or a conductor if it is moved near to the poles of a magnet, in other words, he discovered what we now term electro-magnetic induction. Every schoolboy to-day is familiar with Faraday's simple experiment of thrusting a magnet in and out of a coil of wire, the ends of which are connected to a galvanometer or inductor and watching the needle "kick," showing that a current has been induced in the coil by the movement of the magnet, and yet that discovery demonstrated by that simple experiment is the solid foundation upon which the technical development of the whole of the electrical industry has been built.

title: Commander
brief_context: His Polar expedition used Daventry's wireless broadcasts.
article_title: A New Link with the Empire
brief_extract: Many inventions and discoveries have produced evil results as well as good, but wireless has opened out such immense opportunities for pleasure and enjoyment in which the poorest among us can share, that its influence may be said to be almost wholly for good. We have only to think, too, of Commander Byrd's Polar Expedition; of the lonely camp on the slopes of Everest, where daily messages from home were received on a McMichael "Colonial" Supersonic Short-Wave Receiver from Daventry, or Professor Piccard and his balloon to realise to what perfection wireless communications have attained. But all these are isolated and spectacular happenings.

title: H.M.; King
brief_context: Mentioned for his Christmas Day broadcast message to the Empire.
brief_extract:
It is, of course, at such moments as the
magnificent Christmas Day broadcast with
its culmination in the message by H.M. King George, that the full meaning of Empire
broadcasting is adequately realised. There
is, however, something very moving—senti-
mental, if you like, but then we are all
sentimentalists at heart—in the thought of
those quiet rooms at Broadcasting House,
where British men and women speak to
their fellows overseas, where British culture
and British humour, and the British feeling
for and love of home go winging out on the
invisible waves to be caught who knows
where.

Author of the physics textbook mentioned in the text.
brief_extract: Electric lighting started with arc lamps, and at the present time we are on the eve of returning to arc lamps—of a sort. If we consult such an old-fashioned text book as Ganot's "Physics" we shall see that the electrical section makes reference to Geissler vacuum discharge tubes and the carbon arc. It was known even in these early days that if air was exhausted from a glass tube, a high voltage current could be made to pass through the tube lighting it up with a soft blue-white discharge.

brief_context: Discoverer of X-rays mentioned in the context of vacuum tubes.
brief_extract: It was known even in these early days that if air was exhausted from a glass tube, a high voltage current could be made to pass through the tube lighting it up with a soft blue-white discharge. Such Geissler tubes were little more than scientific toys; but it is of considerable interest to note that eventually these same Geissler tubes led up to the discovery of X-rays and the construction by Röntgen of the first X-ray bulb or tube. In these days the only practical electric light was provided by the carbon arc lamp.

Green
When my friends complained to me of the misplaced loquacity of their dentists—the provocative remark or tantalising question launched upon them when they could not close their mouth to reply—I was often tempted to envy them. McFillem was an excellent dentist, but so economical of speech that beyond the essential "A little wider, please," or "Now rinse," he offered no alleviation or distraction; so that I came to look forward almost eagerly to "Rinse again," and "A little more to the left," while to hear him speak to the nurse was a definite happiness. But last week he surpassed himself.

Washing Day being a ritual in the Lancashire Housewife's home, I ventured to ask about the Electric Wash-boiler, and Mary proudly showed me a small shed her man had made, in which they stored the portable boiler after use. " Is it economical?" I asked, and I was informed that the hire had been paid out of the saving between the old method of gas and the present one of electricity, with a few coppers in hand, to say nothing of the absence of fumes.

title: Countess
brief_context: Subject of the article; runs an electrical showroom business.
brief_extract:
2 APRIL, 1934 No. 16
THE COUNTESS OF BECTIVE
Though she dates her great interest in electrical work from the time when she first moved into a new house, and started housekeeping, Lady Bective has "Always known how to mend a fuse." Coming in contact with business people during this move, and having to make decisions on house decorating and furnishing stimulated her interest in the possibilities of electricity, both for useful and decorative purposes in the home. The showroom of The Bective Electrical Company, Ltd., at 36 Davies Street, W.1, has just celebrated its first birthday, and is proving a wonderful success, part of which Lady Bective modestly attributes to its convenient site.

brief_context: Author of the article on light and colour psychology.
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE 639

LIGHT AND COLOUR

By Maysie Chalmers

Mrs. Pender Chalmers, who combines the work of the Electrical Contractor with that of the Decorative Artist, believes in taking nature as her guide when designing colour schemes.

title: Mrs.
brief_context: Combines work as electrical contractor and decorative artist.
Laid the foundation of the Science of Colour in 1666.
brief_extract: It is however, a perfectly serious question to ask oneself and the answer has an interesting bearing on one's health and happiness. As far back as 1666, Newton laid the foundation of the Science of Colour, when he discovered that, by means of a prism, light could be split up by refraction into an infinite number of parts. Mentioned as an illustrator of Arabian Nights' Entertainment.
brief_extract:
Beneath my left arm I clutched a diary of awe-inspiring dimensions; in my right hand I flourished a fountain pen, determined that nothing which came to my eyes should be trusted to my memory. Those who, in reading this, expect an Arabian Nights' Entertainment with illustrations by Dulac and music by Ketelby, must look elsewhere, for these jottings deal exlusively with the curiously interesting aspect of the far East which the coming of electricity into communities which other-
wise have advanced little for many centuries has brought about. My first glimpse of this juxtaposition of the old and the new was caught at Port Sudan where the Resident Electrical Engineer came on board at seven in the morning and took us on a whirlwind tour.

Beneath my left arm I clutched a diary of awe-inspiring dimensions; in my right hand I flourished a fountain pen, determined that nothing which came to my eyes should be trusted to my memory. Those who, in reading this, expect an Arabian Nights' Entertainment with illustrations by Dulac and music by Ketelby, must look elsewhere, for these jottings deal exlusively with the curiously interesting aspect of the far East which the coming of electricity into communities which other-
wise have advanced little for many centuries has brought about. My first glimpse of this juxtaposition of the old and the new was caught at Port Sudan where the Resident Electrical Engineer came on board at seven in the morning and took us on a whirlwind tour.

article_title: FROM COAL TO GRID: A Visit to Battersea Power Station
brief_extract: First the silence of the Control Room, with its glass bays, where the mere pressing of a tiny button can isolate any danger spot in the fraction of a second. Then the rather terrifying feeling when standing in that same room looking out through those same bays over the great hall, 500 feet long, that here is actually the embodiment of Capek's Robots come to life, but in an even more advanced form, for it is the machines themselves which act with such uncanny foresight, automatically carrying out their jobs without apparent human supervision. We are not surprised to learn that the actual engineering staff for each shift is not much more than two dozen men, for as we go round, room after room is passed with hardly a worker to be seen.

brief_extract: Look at the pans, those there are used every day and taken straight from the cooker to the table, which saves no end—not a mark on them in spite of being used right away since December. My sister from America came over not long ago, and I said to her: 'I don't like you to see the cooker in the sitting room,' but she says to me that it's quite the regular thing over there, and she married more comfortable than me, not that that's always happiness, is it? "What I say is, why shouldn't the working classes have some of the luxuries that the upper classes have, and specially the advantage of electricity in their homes."

THE LADY PENTLAND, D.B.E., J.P. Lady Pentland is a member of the "New Homes for Old" Committee, whose recent housing exhibit at the Building Exhibition, at Olympia, has aroused widespread interest, and where a number of modern working-class kitchens with electrical apparatus are illustrated.

title: Lord
brief_context: Mentioned in relation to the site of a house.
brief_extract: Lady Pentland's first education in domestic science was received in a little wooden house, which her parents handed over to their children, on condition that it was looked after entirely by themselves. Her first experience of electricity was the excitement of seeing electric light installed in the house her parents built in Grosvenor Square, on the site of Lord Shaftesbury's, about 1888. Possibly the recollection of the household labours involved in 'the little wooden house' had an influence when Lady Pentland and her husband bought a house at Hampstead, and determined to make it as work-saving as possible.

title: Miss
brief_context: Writing a history of the Association for its birthday.
brief_extract:
CELEBRATES ITS 10th BIRTHDAY

On November 12th, the Association celebrates its Tenth Birthday and while to those of us who have seen it grown from infancy this should be a time for reviewing early history, it seems more fitting that we should look forward and visualise our future work. Miss Peggy Scott, the well-known journalist, is writing a history of the Association to be published on its Birthday; it will be a revelation to most of our members and certainly to those outside of the enormous amount of work which has been accomplished during the last ten years. As an Association of Women one of our chief aims has been to use all the power that lies within our hands to create better living conditions for those working women and men who most need the great benefits which Electricity can bring and who at present dwell in an atmosphere far from that which may be conducive towards the establishment of a happier and healthier nation.

brief_context: Invented the suction sweeper in Canada 27 years ago.
brief_extract: Behind that invention and its subsequent progress lies a story well worth the telling. Twenty-seven years ago in a small town in Canada, there lived a young man named Murray Spangler. Though somewhat of a mechanical genius, poor health coupled with poverty had compelled him to earn his living as caretaker in the town's main store.

brief_context: Business partner of Murray Spangler who grew the Hoover business.
Original inventor of the vacuum machine who died before completion.
brief_extract: H. Hoover long to recognise the possibilities of Spangler's invention, and the two set up in partnership. Unfortunately Spangler died without seeing the completion of his invention, but his partner carried on.

brief_context: Inventor acknowledged for his contribution to efficient electric cleaning.
brief_extract:
Suction lifts the carpet off the floor and floats it on a cushion of air whilst the agitator beats out the dirt; this is recognised as being the most efficient method of carpet cleaning. This gives some idea of the enormous amount of study and time that has been expended in giving us an efficient Electric Cleaner, and to-day, the millions of women the world over, as they let their electric cleaners do their spring-cleaning for them, owe thanks to Murray Spangler and the band of scientific Engineers, who are ever on the watch for new ideas and improvements to make cleaning an even easier task than it is already. ________________

brief_extract:
Housecraft School Activities
Autumn—Winter 1934

The Housecraft School has a full and varied programme for the coming months, including courses of lectures, practical classes and demonstrations arranged for Teachers, Demonstrators and Housewives, in addition to special lectures arranged for parties of schoolgirls and others visiting headquarters. The Practical Classes for Teachers, held last spring by arrangement with the Battersea Polytechnic, proved so popular that a further series will be held on Tuesday evenings, under the supervision of Miss Dorothy Vaughan, M.C.A. The full equipment of the School is placed at the disposal of those attending the classes, but the number of Teachers is necessarily restricted by the space and apparatus available for their use.

brief_extract:
Birthday Celebrations

Monday, November 12th, 1934, the Tenth Birthday of the Electrical Association for Women, was marked by a number of special events. In the morning, a "history" of the first ten years of its life, written by the journalist, Miss Peggy Scott, was published under the title of "An Electrical Adventure."

In the afternoon, the Marchioness of Reading opened the Exhibition of "Electricity for the Working Woman"; during the tour of the Exhibition, Margaret, Lady Moir, as President, lit the first candle on the magnificent E.A.W. Birthday Cake, made in the Electrical Housecraft School.

title: Marchioness
brief_context: Opened the Exhibition and interpreted the three aims of Electricity.
article_title: FOR THE WORKING WOMAN. Results of the Conference and Exhibition.
brief_extract: Much of the value of our recent Exhibition and Conference on " Electricity for the Working Woman " lay in the chance it gave us of hearing a number of distinguished women discussing the problem from very different angles. The Marchioness of Reading, in opening the Exhibition, interpreted the " three aims of Electricity " as the amelioration of housing conditions, particularly in working class homes ; the lessening of drudgery for all women ; and the practical and profitable application of scientific discoveries to everyday life. Lady Pentland then spoke, to a very large audience, of the work of the London Housing Societies, and gave a very clear view of the great difficulties which they were up against, the problems they have to face, and the ways in which their areas and scope of work is delimited.

title: Lady

article_title: FOR THE WORKING WOMAN. Results of the Conference and Exhibition.
brief_extract: The Marchioness of Reading, in opening the Exhibition, interpreted the " three aims of Electricity " as the amelioration of housing conditions, particularly in working class homes ; the lessening of drudgery for all women ; and the practical and profitable application of scientific discoveries to everyday life. Lady Pentland then spoke, to a very large audience, of the work of the London Housing Societies, and gave a very clear view of the great difficulties which they were up against, the problems they have to face, and the ways in which their areas and scope of work is delimited. We were amazed at the amount of work already achieved, despite these restrictions, in bringing better housing conditions to the really poor.

brief_extract: She had recently returned from America, where she had been particularly struck by the manifold applications of electricity to agriculture on both large and small scales ; she was even more amazed to find that the farm house was as adequately equipped electrically as the farm itself. Miss Elizabeth Craig, too, said that the average American woman took more advantage of electricity than the Englishwoman does. Her first thought is for the perfect equipment of her house, for she knows that only by this means can she give herself the time to enjoy other pleasures.

title: Lady Provost
brief_context: Attended and was pictured at the electrical exhibition.
brief_extract: In connection with the Annual Conference of the National Council of Women of Great Britain, which was held in Edinburgh at the beginning of October, the local Branch of the Association arranged an Exhibition of Electrical Housecraft on Wednesday afternoon, October 3rd. By the kindness of the Principal and Governors of the Heriot Watt College the Exhibition was held in that College and was attended by over 400 men and women, in- cluding the Lady Provost of Edinburgh. Included in the Exhibition were demonstrations of the generation, transmission and distribution of electricity, methods of house wiring, home lighting and decorations by means of coloured lighting, a display of various household electrical appliances, demonstrations of cooking, washing, together with a glimpse into the work of the Association for the housewife, and countrywoman, the teacher and demonstrator.

title: Lady
associated_organisation: Electrical Association for Women, Edinburgh Branch
brief_context: Declared the Electrical Exhibition open and was pictured.
brief_extract: Included in the Exhibition were demonstrations of the generation, transmission and distribution of electricity, methods of house wiring, home lighting and decorations by means of coloured lighting, a display of various household electrical appliances, demonstrations of cooking, washing, together with a glimpse into the work of the Association for the housewife, and countrywoman, the teacher and demonstrator. Lady Elibank, President of the Branch, in declaring the Exhibition open, remarked that women should be grateful for the introduction of electricity into life, for not only had life been eased and much drudgery abolished, but it had also been beautified. What could be more beautiful than Edinburgh Castle lit up at night?

title: Miss
brief_context: Congratulated the branch on the exhibition; pictured.
brief_extract: She expressed the hope that electricity might soon become more economical to use so that it might be brought within the reach of every woman. Miss Caroline Haslett, C.B.E., congratulated the Branch on their enterprise in arranging such an Exhibition, for not only had they gathered together electrical appliances for calculation, but they had given their exhibition a distinctly educational bias. That was, perhaps, not surprising as Scotland and Edinburgh had always been to the front in all questions of education including the educa- tional work of the Association.

title: Mrs.
brief_context: Author of the book The Manchester Man.
Lancashire historian who wrote about Manchester's Cathedral and Hospital.
brief_extract: Linnaeus Banks in The Manchester Man, where she tells how a working couple found a small boy in a basket in the River Irwell, how they looked after him, sent him to the Chetham Hospital Blue-coat School, how he was apprenticed to a cotton merchant, of the Peterloo riots and the stand of the workers for their rights. Nor must we forget the Lancashire historian, Harrison Ainsworth, many of whose writings are concerned with the Cathedral and Chetham’s Hospital where so many of his books were written. In architecture, Manchester hides her light under a bushel, for while there are many beautiful buildings, such as the University, the Town Hall, the Assize Courts, which were all designed by Alfred Waterhouse at the end of the nineteenth century, and the beautiful Rylands Library, yet their beautiful lines and delicate tracery are obscured by the surrounding buildings.

up the home for Easter.

brief_extract: B. Crompton, C.B., the Toast of the evening was to “ A Pioneer,” and a portrait by George Harcourt, R.A., now hanging in the Royal Academy, was presented to this “ Grand Old Man ” of the Electrical World. We have persuaded Colonel Crompton to give us a few of his early memories of the introduction of electricity for domestic purposes.

brief_context: Inventor of the incandescent lamp mentioned in the text.
brief_extract: I think it would be of considerable interest to everyone who is studying the present development of the use of electrical energy, if I tell you of a few of the early difficulties we pioneers met with when we first introduced the use of electricity for lighting purposes. During the few years which preceded Swan’s invention of his lamp, which was the starting point of the supply of electric light in our homes, our work was confined to the development of arc lighting for the illumination of large open spaces, such as railway stations, railway goods yards, docks and quays of harbours. In those days, as the only manufacturers of such apparatus were Siemens and my own firm, we were very proud to be able to show that we got greatly improved effects in steadiness of the light, by using longer arcs than those used by our rivals, Siemens.

brief_context: Rival manufacturer of arc lighting plant mentioned in article.
brief_extract: During the few years which preceded Swan’s invention of his lamp, which was the starting point of the supply of electric light in our homes, our work was confined to the development of arc lighting for the illumination of large open spaces, such as railway stations, railway goods yards, docks and quays of harbours. In those days, as the only manufacturers of such apparatus were Siemens and my own firm, we were very proud to be able to show that we got greatly improved effects in steadiness of the light, by using longer arcs than those used by our rivals, Siemens. In that way we got a much larger percentage of the orders for arc lighting plant than they did.

The diving board of the new swimming pool at Bondor Factory, for staff, men and girls . All-Electric Stocking Factory

WHERE STAFF HAVE HOUSES ELECTRICALLY EQUIPPED

Visited by Annette Adams

In a quaint old Hertfordshire town, which still retains much of its old-time serenity and charm in these bustling days, I visited recently a stocking factory which is run electrically. It is one of the most modern factories in England, and the welfare work for the very large staff is specially noteworthy.

article_title: Women Discuss House Planning and Home Management
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE
939
Women Discuss House Planning
and Home Management
A REPORT OF THE SIXTH INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS FOR SCIENTIFIC MANAGEMENT,
DOMESTIC SECTION
By Muriel Watson
"Scientific Management in the Home" imparts a somewhat formidable note to what is throughout the world the major part of women's daily work. But when one considers average housekeeping of the past as compared with that of today, one realises that "formidable" might more accurately be applied to the daily household tasks carried out by the housewife of forty years ago, and even by the housewife of today who has not adopted the improvements and advantages made possible for her, rather than to that planning and management which can ease and shorten so much that is arduous, and which is science and logic applied to haphazard household routine.
